summary: Discovery/POC scoping focused on integrating DataHarbor's workload with Redwood's benchmark harness. Key discussion points: workload sizing (tokens/request, concurrency), streaming vs non-streaming measurement differences, success criteria (latency p50/p95, cost per 1M tokens, accuracy regression tolerance), test harness integration (k6/Locust scripts, streaming instrumentation), timeline target of a 2-week benchmark run followed by a pilot. transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-08
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marcus Chen (DataHarbor Eng Mgr), Aisha Patel (DataHarbor ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (DataHarbor DevOps), Sofia Ruiz (Product)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro - I'm Jordan, AE on the account, and Priya is our SE who will lead the harness integration stuff. Marcus, do you want to kick off with the goals for today?

[00:18] Marcus Chen: Yeah thanks Jordan. High level we want to run a benchmark POC to validate cost and latency for our summarization pipelines. Specifically we're evaluating streaming responses for our UI vs non-streaming batch responses for backend jobs. We want to understand throughput at our typical concurrency and p95/p99 latency. Also security and staging access questions.

[00:36] Priya Shah: Great. To scope the harness integration I'd like to capture a few things: average tokens per request, peak tokens, concurrency profile (steady vs burst), and whether you have any custom logic in prompts or function/tool-calling that affects response size.

[00:55] Aisha Patel: Rough numbers - avg prompt length ~120 tokens, avg response ~220 tokens, peaks up to 2k for some long document summaries. Concurrency: day-to-day 40-60 concurrent users, peak bursts up to 250 for a few minutes. For background batch jobs we run parallel workers ~100 per cluster.

[01:12] Jordan Lee: Okay that's helpful. So we should plan both interactive streaming tests and non-streaming high-throughput runs. For benchmarks we'll capture token throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, time-to-first-token for streaming, and error rates. Also we usually include a cost estimate per 1M tokens.

[01:33] Liam O'Connor: For the staging side, we'd prefer Redwood hosted endpoints for the initial runs to avoid VPC setup time, but we need to ensure IP allowlist and audit logs, and we want to evaluate Dedicated later. Any gotchas on instrumentation for streaming?

[01:49] Priya Shah: Streaming instrumentation is different - with streaming we measure time-to-first-byte and chunk cadence, whereas non-streaming you measure total latency for full response. Our harness supports both: for streaming we record first-byte latency and also per-chunk timing and aggregate p95 on time-to-first-byte. For load tools we provide examples using k6 + websocket/chunked HTTP wrappers or a simple python async client.

[02:10] Marcus Chen: Can you show an example script?

[02:15] Priya Shah: Sure I'll paste the example in the follow-up note but basically we have a k6 script for non-streaming that hits Redwood endpoints with variable payload sizes, and a python async client that opens a streaming connection and records per-chunk latencies. We also support Locust for more stateful scenarios.

[02:36] Sofia Ruiz: On success criteria our PMs want interactive latency p95 < 300ms for first byte on typical prompts, and full non-streaming jobs p95 < 2s for avg-200-token responses. Cost targets are under $X per 1M tokens - we'll share the exact number after internal calc. Also quality: <3% regression in ROUGE/QA metrics vs our baseline model.

[02:58] Jordan Lee: Good - we can map those to our benchmarks. One thing to call out: streaming first-byte p95 at 300ms is aggressive at high concurrency but we can measure with a baseline config and then tune batching/quantization or move to Dedicated to meet SLOs. We should define baseline model and quantization settings for the test.

[03:18] Aisha Patel: Baseline model is an open Llama-variant we run today; we'll provide model artifacts and sample prompts. For quantization, we're open to trying 8-bit and 4-bit to see perf/cost tradeoffs. Does Redwood's harness support switching quantization knobs?

[03:33] Priya Shah: Yes, the harness can run with different model variants/quant levels; the runtime logs quantization config. For Dedicated tests we can also include GPU type selection in the config so you can compare throughput on A100 vs H100-like instances.

[03:52] Marcus Chen: About data handling - some prompts include PII. For the bench runs we can anonymize, but we need to confirm logs and KV cache retention in Redwood staging. What does Redwood retain in benchmark mode?

[04:06] Jordan Lee: For hosted staging we can enable no-persist mode; we'll also provide the security summary doc. Redwood supports KMS integrations and audit logs for Dedicated/private, but for this POC we can run with minimal retention and masked inputs - we will send the security summary as part of the next steps.

[04:26] Liam O'Connor: Perfect. On the harness side, how do we feed your customer scripts? We have some python clients and a Node.js worker.

[04:35] Priya Shah: We accept scripts as either k6/Locust scenarios or plain python async clients. If you have NodeJS we can wrap it in a small adapter. Best approach is to share a canonical request generator and we'll convert it into a harness scenario. We ask for a sample payload distribution (csv or JSON) and token length histogram.

[04:58] Marcus Chen: We can produce that. About measurement - do you measure CPU/GPU utilization on the Redwood side?

[05:04] Priya Shah: Yes, the harness integrates with our tracing hooks to capture per-request compute and GPU utilization metrics for Dedicated runs. For hosted runs we surface throughput and latency metrics and can provide summary GPU metrics from the run, but low-level host metrics are only available on Dedicated/private due to telemetry constraints.

[05:22] Jordan Lee: One practical point - streaming vs non-streaming affects cost and concurrency. Streaming can reduce perceived latency but increases the number of smaller writes; non-streaming is simpler for batching and GPU efficiency. For your background jobs we might prefer non-streaming with larger batch sizes; for UI interactive sessions streaming makes sense.

[05:44] Aisha Patel: That's exactly our thinking. So for the benchmark we should include three runs: interactive streaming at 60 concurrency, burst 250 concurrency streaming, and batch non-streaming at 100 workers with batched inputs.

[05:58] Priya Shah: That sounds like a good plan. We'll need the sample prompt set and a representative token distribution. Also confirm whether you use function/tool-calling heavily - that changes output size shape.

[06:12] Marcus Chen: We do use function calling for structured extraction on 30% of requests.

[06:18] Priya Shah: Noted. The harness can simulate function-call latencies by returning structured JSON and we'll measure validation success rates as part of quality checks. For accuracy checks we need evaluation prompts and expected outputs; Aisha, could you provide a small eval set (200 samples) for regression detection?

[06:32] Aisha Patel: Yep, we can put together 200 eval samples with expected labels and share them.

[06:36] Jordan Lee: Timeline-wise we recommend: Day 0-2 share artifacts (scripts, sample data, security), Day 3-5 Redwood prep test configs and smoke runs, Day 6-14 run full benchmark matrix and analyze results. So roughly a 2-week run. After that we can discuss pilot/Dedicated timelines. Sound OK?

[06:58] Liam O'Connor: Works for us. One more question: for streaming we want p95 time-to-first-byte - does the harness compute p95 across the client observed distribution or server side?

[07:08] Priya Shah: Client-observed. We run the client workload from our load cluster to simulate your network and measure p50/p95/p99 of time-to-first-byte, plus chunk intervals. We also capture server-side timing where available to correlate.

[07:22] Marcus Chen: If we want to test within our VPC later, is there a recommended approach?

[07:27] Jordan Lee: For VPC/private deployments we usually ship a small agent or run the harness inside your VPC to generate load; we coordinate with your DevOps to open minimal ports and exchange TLS certs. That path will be a follow-up after the hosted runs.

[07:39] Sofia Ruiz: For decision criteria the execs will look at three signals: latency & throughput, cost delta vs baseline, and any accuracy regressions. If those look good, procurement will push for Dedicated evaluation.

[07:52] Priya Shah: Noted. On tools - we will attach example k6 + python streaming clients and a template Locust file. For the streaming python client we instrument time-to-first-byte, chunk counts, and chunk latencies and output to CSV. We can also push results to a shared dashboard.

[08:12] Marcus Chen: Great. Can you also include a small run configuration for quantization experiments? We want to compare fp16, 8-bit, and 4-bit.

[08:20] Priya Shah: Absolutely; we'll include configs and expected tradeoffs; note that 4-bit might increase incoherence for some prompts so we'll run quality checks in parallel.

[08:31] Jordan Lee: Any blocker items on your side?

[08:34] Liam O'Connor: We just need time from our infra team to export sample traces and set up a short access window. Should be okay for the timeline.

[08:41] Aisha Patel: I'll own the eval sample set and the token histogram. Expect that by 2026-04-11.

[08:47] Marcus Chen: Also, please include pricing delta examples for hosted vs Dedicated for the throughput numbers so we can feed into cost-of-ownership discussion.

[08:55] Jordan Lee: Will do. I'll include a simple TCO calc based on your throughput numbers.

[09:00] Sofia Ruiz: Who will run the first smoke test?

[09:03] Priya Shah: Priya and Liam together - I'll run the harness; Liam will validate staging network and token access. We'll coordinate calendar invites in follow-up.

[09:12] Jordan Lee: Okay let's recap next steps and actions. Jordan send pricing and TCO; Priya share harness repo + example scripts; Aisha send eval samples and token histogram; Liam provide staging VPC details and sample load scripts. Meet again after initial smoke - propose 2026-04-14 for the load-run.

[09:34] Marcus Chen: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[09:39] Jordan Lee: Thanks - we'll send notes and links shortly.
